title: The Highest Hands at the Lowest Work
story:
On the last day of the Rajasuya, when the king himself was to be sprinkled with the consecrating waters, the inner enclosure of the sacrificial ground held the most extraordinary assembly the age had gathered. The great brahmana seers had come with the invited kings — rishis who had lived on mountain air and silence, seated now at ease beside thrones, with Narada at their head, he who had seen more ages begin and end than the kings there had counted years. They talked, they debated, they argued philosophy like hawks darting at meat thrown into the air; the enclosure, crowded with gods and seers and kings, shone like the sky thick with stars. No one without vows was near that platform. Yudhishthira's sacrifice had drawn the whole world, and the whole world had come in its best.

Narada looked at the king's prosperity, born of the sacrifice, and was glad. Then he looked at the vast concourse of Kshatriyas — the warriors of a hundred kingdoms, the pride of every royal house in the land — and he grew thoughtful. He remembered words he had heard of old in the mansion of Brahma, when the celestials had been commanded to be born on earth, to meet one another in the field of war, and to return. He knew that this assembly was no mere gathering of princes. It was a concourse of incarnate gods, and the one who moved among them as a man was the one he had known as the source of all things, Narayana, the lord of all, who had taken birth in the line of the Yadavas. The seer sat at the sacrifice of the wise king with feelings of awe, and he saw what no one else in that brilliant hall could see: that this shining gathering was a field being sown for a harvest no one wanted to name.

And into the middle of that glory came the moment the tellers have never forgotten.

Krishna — he who was himself the centre of all worlds, round whom every creature moved — was engaged at his own will in washing the feet of the brahmanas.

He did it himself. The one whom the seers knew as the Self-Create took up the menial office of the sacrifice — the office no proud man would take — and washed the feet of the priests, desirous of excellent fruits, at his own will. No one had asked him. No one could have commanded him. He chose it: the highest bending to the lowest service, and the gesture was so quiet that the old telling records it without fuss, as if it were the most natural thing in the world.

Then Bhishma, the grandsire of the Kurus, rose and addressed Yudhishthira. "Let the arghya be offered to the kings, each as he deserves," he said. "There are six who deserve honor — the preceptor, the sacrificial priest, the relative, the Snataka, the friend, the king. But let the first arghya be offered to the foremost among those present. As the sun among all luminous objects, so is this one among us, in energy, in strength, in prowess. This sacrificial mansion is illuminated and gladdened by him as a sunless region is by the sun, as still air by a breeze."

Yudhishthira asked whom he meant, and Bhishma judged by his intelligence and named Krishna. And at the grandsire's command, Sahadeva duly presented the first arghya of excellent ingredients to Krishna of the Vrishni race, and Krishna accepted it according to the forms of the ordinance.

The hall had seen the lord of all worlds wash the feet of servants; now it saw him raised above all kings. The two honors belonged to the same act, and the whole assembly knew it: the one who served all was fit to be honored by all. For a moment the sacrifice held both images together — the bent back at the water, the raised vessel of honor — and that was the truest thing the Rajasuya showed that day.

But among the seated kings, one had watched the first arghya with a face like a closed fist. His grievance was older than the sacrifice, and it would not wait for the consecration.
reflection: The juxtaposition is the meaning: the same man takes the lowest office in the sacrifice and then receives its highest honor, and no one finds the two in tension. Narada's vision — that the assembly was a concourse of gods gathered to thin the burdened earth — gives the scene its quiet weight: the one serving at the feet of priests is the one who set the whole gathering in motion.
next_story_tease: One king's old grievance, smoldering through the honors, was about to turn the assembly to battle.
hero_scene: In the blazing inner enclosure of the Rajasuya, Krishna kneels at a low basin washing the feet of seated brahmana seers, water spilling over his hands, while behind him the sacrificial platform blazes with golden vessels and the kings of the earth look on.
